Hello Sarah, welcome to the department.

How it works here: a 1:1 with your advisor goes into free time — it does not displace teaching or governance duties — and a meeting counts as booked only once it is on both calendars (his and yours). The office keeps the official schedule but does not arrange people's meetings, so you propose a time to Professor Alvarez and he confirms it.

Two rules worth knowing as a new member: official events are fixed, and a cancellation counts only when this office confirms it in writing — "someone told me it's cancelled" is not enough.

From the official schedule, the windows next week with no official commitment of Professor Alvarez (Mon-Fri, 09:00-17:00):
- Mon: 10:00-13:00, 14:00-14:30
- Tue: 11:00-12:20, 14:20-16:30
- Wed: 10:00-13:30, 15:00-16:30
- Thu: 10:00-10:30, 11:50-14:20, 15:20-16:10
- Fri: 10:00-12:30

These are free of official events only — I don't know his private appointments, so he still needs to agree. A 30-minute slot fits anywhere in those windows.

Hi Sarah — welcome!

Procedure: you write to Professor Alvarez directly to find a time. The department office keeps the official schedule (lectures, seminars, office hours, committees, department meetings), so you don't book your 1:1 through them; if you ever need to check whether an official event is really cancelled or moved, that's who confirms it in writing.

What the handbook asks you to respect when picking a slot:

- Working hours are Mon-Fri, 09:00-17:00 — nothing outside that.
- **Your** 1:1 with your advisor goes into **your free time**, not over your lectures, sections, office hours, seminars or other fixed commitments. Same for the professor: teaching and governance duties come before a 1:1, so don't propose a time that sits on their lecture, office hours, senate or committee meeting.
- A meeting counts as booked only when every participant has it on their calendar. So agree the slot, put it in your calendar, and make sure they've confirmed and put it in theirs.
- Log every change to your own calendar.

So: check your own free half-hours next week, propose one or two to the professor, and confirm. Good luck!

— John
